title: Understanding next.config
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and boundaries of Understanding next.config in the context of Request Processing, Proxy, and Configuration.
Apply Configuring allowed assets in a minimal JavaScript/JSX or configuration example and describe its expected result.
Verify the example with one relevant edge or failure case and identify version/runtime assumptions.

content.intro: This lesson develops Understanding next.config in the supplied Next.js curriculum. The list below preserves its named syllabus subtopics and ties them to a small example you can inspect and adapt.
content.why_it_matters: Request-time code runs at a network boundary before rendering. In Next.js 16 the convention is Proxy; use it selectively, not as a substitute for authorization. In practice, configuring allowed assets should be understood well enough to explain the expected behavior and how it can fail.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Request-time code runs at a network boundary before rendering. In Next.js 16 the convention is Proxy; use it selectively, not as a substitute for authorization. Use “Understanding next.config” to connect the framework convention to observable behavior. Identify the inputs, the boundary where the work runs, and the evidence that confirms it works.

items.title: Configuring allowed assets
items.text: For configuring allowed assets, preserve layout stability, provide accessible text where needed, and load only the resources the page requires.

items.title: Build and output settings
items.text: “Build and output settings” is part of the lesson model for Understanding next.config. Describe its role, use the framework convention that applies to the selected Next.js version, and confirm the result with a focused example.

items.title: Redirects and rewrites
items.text: For redirects and rewrites, connect the URL and filesystem convention to the rendered result and verify direct navigation as well as client-side transitions.

content_blocks.expected_output: A request for /old redirects to /new. In Next.js 16, the file convention is proxy.js; legacy middleware.js is covered only for older releases.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This is an inspectable example, not an arbitrary-code runner inside CodeLeaf. Start from a separate JavaScript App Router project created with `npx create-next-app@latest my-next-app --js --app`, put the snippet in the named or relevant file, and run `npm run dev`. Examples that call application-owned helpers, databases, authentication, or third-party APIs require those dependencies and appropriate environment variables. Use `npm run build` to validate a production build after adapting it.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet, reset the example data and request state, then rerun the same normal case and one empty, invalid, slow, denied, or failed case as relevant. Remove any test records and use non-production credentials.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through “Understanding next.config” by predicting the result before running the example. Identify which file convention or API creates the behavior, then vary one relevant input such as a route parameter, form value, request result, or viewport. Record the actual outcome and compare it with the expected result above.

content_blocks.title: Version and environment note
content_blocks.text: This JavaScript-first course uses the Next.js 16 documentation snapshot checked on 2026-10-18. Version note: in Next.js 16 the `middleware` convention is deprecated and renamed to `proxy`. The Pages Router/Middleware details belong in the legacy track only. TypeScript is an optional parallel skill, not a requirement for these examples. Confirm any experimental or configuration-dependent API in the exact version installed in your learning project.

content.task: Create or inspect a minimal example for “Understanding next.config”. Include the syllabus concept “Configuring allowed assets”, state its expected output, and verify one normal and one boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named concept rather than only mentioning it.
Expected output and the project/runtime needed to reproduce it are documented.
At least one boundary, empty, loading, denied, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
Secrets and trusted server operations stay on the server; UI behavior remains semantic and accessible where relevant.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Configuring allowed assets”.
Predict the output, change one input at a time, and compare the result with your expectation.
If results differ, check the route/file convention, current Next.js and Node.js versions, server logs, and whether the behavior is cache-dependent.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a development preview as proof that the production application is correct.
common_mistakes.why: Caching, environment configuration, deployment constraints, and error handling can differ between development and production.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the relevant targeted tests and a production build, then verify the deployed/runtime-specific behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Relying on client-only checks for sensitive data or mutations.
common_mistakes.why: Requests can be sent without using the visible UI.
common_mistakes.fix: Authenticate, authorize, validate inputs, and check resource ownership inside the trusted server operation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a Next.js behavior is universal across releases.
common_mistakes.why: Rendering, caching, config, and request processing APIs evolve between versions.
common_mistakes.fix: Name the target release and check its matching official docs before publishing or upgrading the example.

summary: Understanding next.config fits into Request Processing, Proxy, and Configuration and should be explained with the vocabulary in the syllabus subtopics.
Keep the implementation minimal, make its runtime boundary explicit, and document its expected output.
Verify at least one relevant edge/failure case before treating the example as correct.
